e.etymology: A respelling of Eliana, understood as Hebrew for 'my God has answered'. Eliana is also the Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of the Roman name Aeliana.
A respelling of Messiah, from Hebrew mashiach, 'anointed one', the title Christians give to Jesus. The spelling also echoes Isaiah and Josiah.
e.note: As a form of Messiah, a title Christians reserve for Jesus, the name strikes some people as irreverent.

e.etymology: An American double name joining Emmy, a pet form of Emma and Emily, to Lou, from Louise. The singer Emmylou Harris made the one-word form familiar.

assoc.t: Emmylou Harris, country and folk singer
Emmylou, 2012 song by First Aid Kit

e.etymology: A modern Indian name from Sanskrit deva, 'god', and amsha, 'part, portion': a portion of the divine.
A modern name popular in Pakistan and with Pakistani American families. Its roots are not well documented.
A modern name used by South Asian Muslim families, also written Izaan. It drew attention in 2018 when tennis star Sania Mirza and cricketer Shoaib Malik chose it for their son.
The Spanish and Italian form of Frederick, through medieval Latin Fredericus from Germanic words for 'peace' and 'ruler'.
namesakes: Federico García Lorca (Spanish poet and playwright)

e.meaning: grace; God is my oath (Anna plus Lisa)
e.etymology: An Italian compound of Anna, from Hebrew for 'grace', and Lisa, a short form of Elisabetta (Elizabeth), 'my God is an oath'. German Anneliese and Scandinavian Anne-Lise are built the same way.
A form of Augustine used in French, German and Romanian, from Latin Augustinus, a derivative of Augustus, 'venerable'. Saint Augustine of Hippo made the name famous.
A respelling of Cadence, the English word for rhythm and for the close of a musical phrase, from Latin cadere, 'to fall'.
A modern coinage also spelled Kya and Kaia. It has no single source and follows the sound of Maya, Kyla and Kyra.
A spelling of Ellery, an English surname that came from the medieval first name Hilary, from Latin hilaris, 'cheerful'.
Usually taken as a form of Khalila, the feminine of Arabic Khalil, 'close friend'. Kalila is also a character in Kalila wa Dimna, the classic Arabic book of animal fables.
The English word, from Old English mona. Moon is also an English surname and a common spelling of the Korean surname Mun.
namesakes: Moon Unit Zappa (actress, daughter of Frank Zappa)

assoc.t: to moon someone: to bare one's backside as a prank

e.note: To moon someone is slang for baring your backside at them.

e.etymology: From the English title earl, Old English eorl, 'nobleman, warrior'. It also became a surname for people who served in an earl's household.
namesakes: Earl Warren (Chief Justice of the United States)
Earl Campbell (Hall of Fame running back)

assoc.t: earl, a rank of British nobility
Earl Hickey, lead of the sitcom My Name Is Earl
Earl Grey, the bergamot-scented black tea
Goodbye Earl, 2000 hit by The Chicks

e.etymology: An old American pet name connected with Arlene, Arthur and the surname Arley. It was given to both boys and girls around 1900 and has returned for girls alongside Harley and Marley.

e.meaning: from Laurentum, an ancient Roman town
e.etymology: The Scandinavian form of Laurentius (Lawrence), 'man from Laurentum', in use since the Middle Ages. Laurentum's own name is usually linked to the laurel tree.
From Arabic malika, 'queen', the feminine of malik, 'king'.
From Sanskrit samartha, 'capable, competent, powerful'. It is also an honorific, as in Samarth Ramdas, the 17th-century Marathi saint.

e.meaning: dweller by a stile, steps over a fence
e.etymology: From an English surname for someone who lived near a stile, a set of steps over a fence or wall, from Old English stigel. Stiles Stilinski of the TV series Teen Wolf brought it into use as a first name.

assoc.t: Stiles Stilinski, sidekick in MTV's Teen Wolf

e.etymology: A short form of Christina and of other names ending in -tina, such as Martina, Valentina and Albertina. It has been given as a full name since the 20th century.

assoc.t: Tina Turner, the Queen of Rock 'n' Roll
Tina, the eldest kid on Bob's Burgers

e.etymology: A spelling of Carly, a feminine form of Carl that came into use in the later 20th century and also a pet form of Carla and Carlotta. Carl comes from Germanic karl, 'free man'.
From Hebrew tamar, 'date palm'. Two women in the Hebrew Bible bear the name: the daughter-in-law of Judah and a daughter of King David. Queen Tamar ruled Georgia at its medieval height.
namesakes: Tamar Braxton (R&B singer and TV personality)

e.etymology: A short name with several sources: a spelling of Vaughn, a clipping of names such as Devon and Lavon, and the German word von, 'of, from', the marker of noble surnames.

assoc.t: von, the 'of' in German noble surnames
King Von, Chicago drill rapper killed in 2020

e.etymology: From Sanskrit shreya, the feminine of a name based on shreyas, 'best, excellent, auspicious'. It is also counted among the names of the goddess Lakshmi.

e.meaning: illusion in Sanskrit; water in Hebrew
e.etymology: A respelling of Maya, a name with many sources: Sanskrit maya, 'illusion'; a Hebrew name linked to mayim, 'water'; and Maia, a Greek nymph and Roman goddess of spring.
A modern name used by Mexican and Mexican American families, usually described as Maya-inspired like Yatzil and Itzel. No firm derivation is documented.
A modern American name, an offshoot of names ending in -riyah such as Mariyah and Zariyah, also seen as a spelling of Ria or Riya.
The English word, from Latin natura, 'birth, character, the order of the world'. As a name it belongs with modern word names such as Journey and Heaven.
Invented by author George R. R. Martin for Princess Rhaenyra Targaryen in his Westeros histories. HBO's House of the Dragon, which began in 2022, brought it into use for real children.
namesakes: Rhaenyra Targaryen (House of the Dragon heir to the Iron Throne)

assoc.t: Rhaenyra Targaryen, dragon queen in House of the Dragon

e.etymology: A form in the family of Lena, Leanna and Liana, recorded in the US since the 1800s. It has no separate meaning of its own; Leanna joins Lee and Anna, and Liana is short for names like Juliana.
namesakes: Leana Wen (physician and public health commentator)

e.etymology: A modern respelling of Brantley, an English surname used as a first name. Brantley climbed in the 2010s alongside country singer Brantley Gilbert.
